questions.q: 'You ___ work hard if you want a seat in IIT.' Fill with should/must/may and justify.
questions.a: 'must' — necessity for a required goal; 'should' understates it as optional advice. A wrong answer 'should' reveals the student grades obligation by politeness rather than by consequence — boards mark the stronger obligation correct when the outcome is non-negotiable.

questions.q: '___ I borrow your pen?' — polite, formal permission. Which modal?
questions.a: 'May' (or 'Could' for polite request). 'Can I borrow' is informal. A wrong answer showing no awareness of the register difference reveals the student thinks modals differ only in meaning, not in formality level.

questions.q: 'It ___ rain tomorrow — the sky is clear.' Choose may/must/should.
questions.a: The clear sky undercuts certainty — 'may' (possibility) or better 'might'. 'Must rain' claims certainty the context denies. A wrong answer 'must' reveals the student reads modals as filler and ignores the evidential clue in the sentence.

questions.q: Modals are function words — each encodes a specific ______ job: ability (can/could), permission (may/can/could), obligation (must/should/ought to), possibility (may/might/could), request (would/could/will).

What is Modals? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Modals are function words — each encodes a specific communicative job: ability (can/could), permission (may/can/could), obligation (must/should/ought to), possibility (may/might/could), request (would/could/will).

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Modals?
questions.a: Students treat modals as interchangeable politeness decorations, pick by 'sounds right' — usually overusing 'can' and 'should' — and believe 'must' and 'should' are synonyms.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Given a context, the student selects the modal matching the intended function (advice vs obligation vs permission vs possibility) and can articulate the nuance difference between near-synonyms (must/should, may/might).
